title: Enrichment, Initiative and the Golden Time Dilemma
author: Samuel Kammin
summary: Samuel Kammin's twenty-second School Notes visits Cranford Park, a small Church of England primary in Hampshire, to ask what distinguishes purposeful enrichment from extra free time. He first traces the English policy background from SMSC and pupil voice to the current enrichment framework and the push on oracy. At the school he describes Cranford Park University, a mixed-age weekly programme of themed faculties that replaced Golden Time, which the headteacher called a waste of time. He explores the tension between structured enrichment and free play, and the problem of making valued activities conditional on behaviour. He acknowledges trade-offs, including the risk of an engagement illusion and the practical limits of staffing and budget. He concludes that enrichment matters only when paired with worthwhile knowledge.
points: Kammin separates planned, structured enrichment from unstructured free time, arguing the former can introduce unfamiliar interests and build initiative.
The headteacher's critique of Golden Time raises the question of whether play and social time should be contingent on good behaviour.
He cautions that an impressive product, like a Tudor house model, is not proof that pupils understand the history behind it.
He flags delivery as a real constraint, since staffing, space and transport costs can turn enrichment into a postcode lottery.
He ties enrichment back to knowledge, insisting that confident, resourceful children also need something worth knowing.
quotes: At a rudimentary level, it is difficult to avoid treating school enrichment as something of an add-on, something extra, which is why ‘extra-curricular’ is a such a natural synonym.
It replaces Golden Time, which the headteacher dismissed as “just a waste of time”.

Free play can provide opportunities for imagination, friendship and social engagement, while planned and structured enrichment opportunities such as the Cranford Park University can introduce children to unfamiliar interests, develop practical skills and encourage initiative.

Removing opportunities for play and social interaction has been well documented to be particularly counterproductive for children who struggle with behaviour or self regulation, so perhaps this would end up being a lose-lose in the long run.

Of course, there is a trade-off here that we should be mindful of - it is important to ensure that the activity deepens children’s understanding rather than simply making the lesson more entertaining.
A beautifully constructed Tudor house is not necessarily evidence that the children understand Tudor society.
There is also the practical problem of delivery. Schools may want to offer a broad range of experiences but lack the staff, space, transport budgets or external partnerships to make them happen.

Enrichment is a tricky business to get right, but it matters because education must prepare children to think and act well, not simply accumulate inert facts, while recognising that meaningful thinking depends on having something worth knowing.
